s: A. Framework.
The Equal Protection Clause binds states.
The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause imposes an identical equal protection requirement on the federal government (Bolling v. Sharpe, 1954, "reverse incorporation").
Every law classifies, so the question is which classifications demand justification.
Equal protection analysis.
Identify the classification.
Facial: the law draws the line in its terms.
Facially neutral laws trigger heightened scrutiny only with proof of discriminatory purpose.
Disparate impact alone is not enough (Washington v. Davis, 1976).
Purpose means a decision made "because of, not merely in spite of" its effects (Personnel Administrator v. Feeney, 1979).
Courts infer it from impact, history, procedural departures, and contemporaneous statements (Arlington Heights, 1977).
Discriminatory application of a neutral law (Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 1886).
Choose the tier.
Strict scrutiny applies to race, national origin, alienage (state laws) and fundamental rights.
Intermediate scrutiny applies to sex and nonmarital children.
Rational basis applies to everything else.
Apply the tier to ends and means.
The government's interest must be compelling, important, or legitimate.
The fit must be narrow tailoring, a substantial relationship, or a rational relationship.
The burden is on the government under heightened scrutiny and on the challenger under rational basis.
